analysis.one_liner: Prohibits paying lower wages in female- or minority-dominated jobs for equivalent work.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Labor Committee without a hearing or a vote; no chamber ever acted on it.
analysis.plain_summary: The Fair Pay Act would have extended equal-pay law beyond jobs that are identical to jobs that are 'equivalent' — different work, but comparable skill, effort, responsibility, and conditions. Employers could not pay jobs dominated by women or racial minorities less than jobs dominated by white men that are equivalent, unless the gap came from seniority, merit, or production systems. It would also have required larger employers to report wage data to the EEOC by race and sex, protected workers who discuss their wages, and let equal-pay lawsuits proceed as class actions with expert fees covered for winning plaintiffs.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in jobs dominated by women or racial minorities — fields like caregiving, clerical work, and service jobs that historically paid less than equivalent male-dominated work. The bill targeted the 'comparable worth' gap: it aimed to raise pay where an employer's own wage-setting systematically undervalued female- and minority-dominated jobs, and its findings cited federal studies finding large unexplained wage gaps between white and non-white workers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women and workers of color in undervalued jobs

how_it_helps.text: Bars employers from paying workers in a job dominated by one sex, race, or national origin less than workers in an equivalent job dominated by a different group, with exceptions only for seniority, merit, or production-based systems.

Allows equal-pay suits to be brought as class actions and requires courts to award expert-witness fees to prevailing plaintiffs, making it easier for individual workers to challenge entrenched pay gaps.
Protects employees who ask about, disclose, or discuss wages from retaliation, and outlaws retaliation against workers who oppose or help investigate pay discrimination.

Requires employers of 15 or more employees to report wage rates by sex, race, and national origin to the EEOC, making systematic pay gaps visible, with small-business exemptions and confidentiality safeguards.
Bars employers from complying by cutting anyone's wage — pay gaps must be closed upward.

analysis.who_pays: Employers whose wage structures pay equivalent female- or minority-dominated jobs less — they would face back-pay liability, required wage adjustments upward, and new recordkeeping and EEOC reporting duties.

drawbacks.text: Compliance would be costly and contentious: employers with 15 or more employees must file detailed wage reports by race and sex, and courts would have to judge whether dissimilar jobs are 'equivalent' based on EEOC guidelines, inviting litigation and disputes over how jobs are valued.

The bill relies on regulators to define 'job dominated by' a group by guideline rather than statute, leaving the exact scope of liability uncertain until the EEOC acted — an honest cost for employers and courts alike.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core trade-off is straightforward: it would raise pay for millions of workers in historically undervalued jobs at real cost to the employers who benefit from those lower wages. The reporting and litigation costs are real but the bill buffers them with small-business exemptions, confidentiality protections, a ban on complying by cutting anyone's pay, and preserved seniority, merit, and production systems. The harder question is legal, not moral: whether 'equivalent jobs' can be compared fairly without regulators misvaluing work.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read once and referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or voted on it before the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Harkin and eight Democratic colleagues introduced the Fair Pay Act of 1997 on January 29, 1997.
The bill's only recorded action beyond introduction was referral to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources the same day.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, floor action, or roll call ever followed; the bill sat in committee until the Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers with pay structures that undervalue female- and minority-dominated jobs were better off, because the bill's higher-wage and reporting requirements never took effect. Workers in those jobs were worse off, having gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Pay Act of 1997 and delivered introductory remarks on it.

for.name: 8 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including original sponsors named in the bill text (Leahy, Boxer, Murray, Inouye, Mikulski, Kerry).

against.name: Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and never scheduled a hearing or markup; no action occurred for the rest of the 105th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All nine senators attached to the bill — the sponsor and every cosponsor — were Democrats, and no Republican support is recorded; the bill then died in a committee chaired by a Republican without any vote.

industries.industry: Large employers in female- and minority-dominated fields (healthcare, care work, clerical, retail services)
industries.note: These employers would have had to raise wages in jobs they had historically paid less because they were staffed mostly by women or minorities, and file wage data with the EEOC. Their interest in blocking the bill ran against the workers whose pay would rise.
The bill exempts small employers from EEOC wage reporting in early years (25+ employees at first, 15+ after), but they remain subject to the equal-pay prohibition itself once they reach those sizes.
